Below are five AI-generated responses to the same task, labelled A through E.

Each response was written by one of these five language models:
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

For each of the five responses, identify which model you believe wrote it, judging only from writing style, structure, and phrasing.

Answer independently for each response. Your five answers do not need to be five different models - name whichever model you believe wrote each response, even if that means naming the same model more than once.

Reply with JSON only, in exactly this form and nothing else:

{
  "A": {"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"},
  "B": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "C": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "D": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "E": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."}
}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- RESPONSE A ---
The Moon appears to go through phases because it orbits Earth while reflecting sunlight, so only half of it is ever lit at once. From our viewpoint on Earth, the angle between the Sun, Moon, and our planet constantly shifts as the Moon moves along its path, revealing changing portions of that illuminated half. When the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun its dark side faces us, producing a new moon, whereas the opposite alignment shows the fully lit side as a full moon; the cycle repeats roughly every month.

--- RESPONSE B ---
The Moon appears to go through phases because of its orbit around Earth and the changing angles at which sunlight reflects off its surface. As the Moon moves, different portions of its sunlit side become visible from Earth, creating the cycle of phases from New Moon to Full Moon and back. This happens because the Moon does not produce its own light but reflects sunlight, and Earth’s perspective changes as the Moon orbits.

--- RESPONSE C ---
The Moon appears to go through phases because as it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half. The Sun always lights up one side of the Moon, but from Earth our viewing angle changes, making the Moon look full, partly lit, or nearly dark.

--- RESPONSE D ---
The Moon doesn't produce its own light; it shines by reflecting sunlight, so only the half facing the Sun is ever illuminated. As the Moon orbits Earth over about a month, we see varying portions of that lit half from our vantage point, which creates the familiar cycle of phases. When the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, its dark side faces us (new moon), and when Earth sits between the Sun and Moon, we see the fully lit side (full moon), with crescent, quarter, and gibbous shapes appearing at points in between.

--- RESPONSE E ---
The Moon appears to go through phases because it orbits the Earth, which constantly changes our viewing angle of its sunlit side. While the Sun always illuminates exactly half of the Moon, the amount of that lit portion we can see from Earth changes as the Moon moves. Consequently, we see different fractions of the bright side over the course of a month, creating the appearance of changing shapes.

--- END OF RESPONSES ---
Now output the JSON object described above, and nothing else.
